title: What Carpentry Is
description: Carpentry is the craft of cutting, joining, and finishing wood into useful things. This flagship record defines the craft, names its core skills, and points to the project pairs that teach each skill by building. The practice board cut list below is a small sample piece for trying a first straight cut, a first square mark, and a first glued joint, and it carries no load.

    total_bf += bf
    print("%s: %.2f board feet" % (name, bf))
print("Total board feet: %.2f" % total_bf)
print("With 10%% waste allowance: %.2f board feet" % (total_bf * 1.10))
print("Total pieces: %d" % 1)

title: Core Carpentry Skills Overview
description: The core skills are measuring, marking, sawing to a line, drilling square, joining, gluing, sanding, and finishing. Each skill is practiced alone on a sample board before it is trusted on a real project, and each project record names which skills it needs and which skill level it honestly requires. A builder who can measure twice, cut once, and keep a square edge can build everything in the simple ladder.

title: Workshop Safety Overview
description: Eye protection is worn for every cut, sanding pass, and hammer blow, because a single chip can end a builder's sight. Hearing protection is worn for power saws and routers, dust is collected or masked against, blades are guarded and unplugged before any adjustment, cords are kept out of walkways, and offcuts are cleared before the next cut. No step in any record in this suite ever asks a builder to remove a guard, reach over a blade, or work while tired or rushed, and any record that involves a blade repeats its blade rule on that record.

title: Measuring Basics
description: Accurate measuring means reading a tape or rule to the sixteenth of an inch, marking with a sharp pencil or knife line, and checking the mark before cutting. The builder measures from the same end every time, marks the waste side of the line with an X, and cuts on the waste side so the kept piece stays true to size. A second measurement after cutting catches drift early, and the demo below converts the practice board between inches and millimetres so both systems stay honest.

title: Marking and Layout Basics
description: Layout turns numbers on a plan into lines on wood. A combination square marks right angles and checks edges, a marking gauge scores a line parallel to an edge for a joint or a rip, and measuring both diagonals of a frame proves it square when the two diagonals match. Lines are marked on the face that will show, and the builder works from a single reference edge so small errors do not stack across a project.

title: Wood Selection Basics
description: Wood choice follows use. Soft pine is cheap and easy to cut, which suits practice and painted work, but it dents easily. Poplar is smooth and stable for painted furniture. Oak is hard and strong for table tops and chair frames, and its open grain shows through a clear finish. Cedar resists weather outdoors and is light, but it is soft and splits if screws are driven near an end without a pilot hole. Boards are sighted along their length for bow and twist before buying, and the straightest boards are saved for the longest pieces.

title: Reading a Cut List and Plan
description: A cut list names every piece, its finished size, and how many are needed. The builder reads it in full before cutting, groups pieces by thickness so one saw setup cuts them all, and cuts the longest pieces first so a mistake on a short piece does not waste a long board. Every record in this suite carries its cut list in this form, with an arithmetic note stating how the pieces add up, so the list can be checked with the demo before any wood is cut.

title: Hand Tools Overview
description: The hand tools that build most of this suite are a handsaw, a chisel set, a hand plane, a mallet, a square, a tape, and a marking knife. Sharpness is the whole secret: a sharp chisel pares cleanly with hand pressure, while a dull chisel needs a mallet blow and slips. Work is always clamped or held in a vise before a tool touches it, hands stay behind the cutting edge, and a plane is pushed with the grain, never against it, to avoid tear-out.

title: Joinery Overview
description: Joinery is how wood pieces hold each other. A butt joint is two square ends glued and screwed, and it suits simple boxes. A pocket-screw joint hides the screw in an angled hole and suits fast frames. A mortise and tenon locks a rail into a leg and suits chairs and tables that take racking force. A dovetail locks a drawer box against pulling force, and a dado groove carries a shelf so the shelf cannot sag off its screws. Each joinery guide in the suite teaches one joint fully, and each project record names the joints it uses.

title: Gluing and Clamping Basics
description: A good glue joint needs close-fitting surfaces, a thin even coat of glue on both faces, firm clamping, and a full cure before the clamps come off or the piece is stressed. Squeeze-out is wiped with a damp cloth before it dries, because dried glue blocks stain and finish. Joints are dry-fitted first without glue so the clamp positions are known, and the builder checks for square while the glue is still wet, when a frame can still be pushed square.

title: Sanding and Surface Preparation
description: Sanding runs through grits from coarse to fine: 80 to remove mill marks, 120 to smooth, 180 to refine, and 220 for furniture that will take a clear finish. Each pass runs with the grain, never across it, because cross-grain scratches show under finish. Dust is brushed and wiped away between grits, and a hand feels the surface after the last grit, since a hand finds a ridge that eyes miss. Edges are eased lightly so a sharp corner does not chip or cut a hand.

title: Finishing Basics Overview
description: Finishing protects wood and shows its grain. Oil is wiped on thin, left to soak, and wiped off, which gives a natural hand-rubbed feel but little scratch resistance. Polyurethane builds a hard film that resists water and wear on table tops, and it is sanded lightly between coats. Paint covers the grain entirely and suits pine and poplar, and wax over oil gives a soft sheen. Every coat is applied thin, because a thick coat runs, bubbles, and cures soft, and oily rags are laid flat outdoors to dry, never bunched, because bunched oil rags can catch fire.

title: Building Your First Project: A Practice Board Plan
description: A first project should be small, square, and forgiving. This practice table has a flat top, four legs, and four aprons, built with butt joints and screws so no advanced joint is needed. The builder measures and cuts all nine pieces, dry-fits the frame, checks both diagonals for square, glues and screws the aprons to the legs, fixes the top, sands through the grits, and finishes with oil or paint. Mistakes are expected on a first build, and the design tolerates them: a slightly short apron still fits inside the frame, and a sanded top hides a saw mark.

title: The Family Framework: From Simple to Complex Builds
description: The family framework is the ladder the whole suite climbs. Simple builds use straight cuts and butt joints, and they teach measuring and square assembly. Compounded builds add one new skill, such as a dado, a pocket screw, an angle, or a drawer, on top of the simple skills. Complex builds combine joints, angles, and fitted parts, such as a chair that must stay square under a sitter's weight or a wardrobe whose doors must hang true. Every record in every pair carries its ladder rank and its honest skill level, so a builder never meets a complex joint without warning.
